questions.stem: Which instruction best reduces choking risk when feeding a toddler?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Offer hard candy and whole nuts as routine snacks because these foods strengthen chewing skills","B":"Serve whole grapes and round hot-dog slices because chewing ability is mature once a toddler walks","C":"Allow eating while walking or playing because movement does not meaningfully change choking risk","D":"Prepare foods in developmentally safe shapes and sizes and avoid small, hard, round choking hazards"}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends preparing food to an age-appropriate size, shape, and texture, avoiding small/hard foods, cutting spherical foods such as grapes into small pieces, and supervising children while eating.
questions.source_detail: Infant and Toddler Nutrition, Choking Prevention and Potential Choking Hazards; March 11, 2026; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: Before crushing a tablet for administration through an enteral feeding tube, what should the nurse verify?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Whether the dosage form can be safely manipulated; modified-release and enteric-coated products may not be crushable","B":"Whether the tablet is large enough to crush; formulation design does not affect tube-administration safety","C":"Whether tube feeding is running, because all solid oral medications are safe to crush when nutrition is infusing","D":"Whether the client can taste the medicine, because taste determines whether a tablet can be crushed safely"}}
questions.rationale: Medication suitability must be checked before crushing for tube administration. Modified-release and enteric-coated products are common examples that may be inappropriate to crush because manipulation can alter release, efficacy, safety, or tube patency.
questions.source_name: PubMed — Developing Guidance for Feeding Tube Administration of Oral Medications
questions.source_detail: JPEN 2023, PMID 36847617: evaluation of oral dosage forms for feeding-tube administration and appropriateness of crushing/manipulation; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A critically ill client must travel to another hospital department for a procedure. Which transport plan best supports safety?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Send the client without monitoring when the destination is nearby and the expected trip is brief","B":"Use appropriate monitoring, transport equipment, emergency capability, and qualified accompanying personnel","C":"Leave emergency equipment on the unit because the receiving department assumes all transport risk","D":"Use an untrained escort if vital signs were stable at the moment the client left the intensive-care unit"}}
questions.rationale: Critical-care transport guidelines call for a formal process addressing pretransport coordination, appropriate transport equipment, monitoring, qualified personnel, and documentation because transport carries inherent risk.
questions.source_name: American College of Critical Care Medicine/SCCM — Transport of Critically Ill Patients
questions.source_detail: Guideline abstract: transport personnel, equipment, monitoring, communication, and documentation; Crit Care Med 2004; PMID 14707589; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A client is on droplet precautions for a respiratory infection. How is the duration of transmission-based precautions determined?

questions.rationale: CDC states that Transmission-Based Precautions remain in effect while transmission risk persists, with duration depending on the pathogen, clinical course, testing, treatment, and applicable facility or public-health guidance.

questions.stem: A nurse administers an antineoplastic hazardous drug. Which PPE approach is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Omit PPE when a closed-system device is available because engineering controls eliminate all exposure risk","B":"Use a surgical mask alone because ventilation eliminates skin and mucous-membrane exposure to hazardous drugs","C":"Use ordinary examination gloves alone because chemotherapy-rated gloves are needed only for drug compounding","D":"Use chemotherapy gloves and a protective gown, adding eye, face, or respiratory protection as exposure risk requires"}}
questions.rationale: NIOSH recommends chemotherapy gloves and a nonabsorbent protective gown for antineoplastic drug handling, with additional eye/face or respiratory protection according to the task and exposure risk. Engineering controls supplement rather than automatically eliminate PPE needs.
questions.source_name: CDC/NIOSH — Chemical Hazards Risk Factors: Antineoplastic Drugs
questions.source_detail: Healthcare worker controls: chemotherapy gloves, nonabsorbent gown, and task-specific additional controls; Aug. 12, 2024 with 2026 hazardous-drug resources; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A facility permits a routine laboratory specimen to be sent through its validated pneumatic tube system. What should the nurse do before sending it?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Seal and label the specimen correctly and use the facility-approved leak-resistant transport packaging","B":"Loosen the container cap so pressure changes during transit can escape through the specimen opening","C":"Remove patient identification because the pneumatic carrier itself provides adequate specimen identity","D":"Place an unsealed specimen directly in the carrier because tube systems prevent leakage by design"}}
questions.rationale: Specimens must be properly identified and transported in secure, leak-resistant containers according to laboratory and facility policy. Pneumatic systems require validation for the specimen type; some high-risk specimens should not be sent by pneumatic tube.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guidelines for Safe Work Practices in Diagnostic Laboratories
questions.source_detail: Specimen transport: leakproof primary container and sealable leakproof transport packaging; MMWR Suppl. 2012; accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: A family member asks whether a bed-exit alarm physically keeps a high-risk client in bed. Which response is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It mechanically restrains the client in bed and therefore replaces all other individualized fall interventions","B":"It alerts staff to movement or attempted bed exit but does not physically prevent the client from leaving","C":"It locks the bed rails in place and prevents voluntary movement until a nurse deactivates the device","D":"It eliminates fall risk once activated, so reassessment and a tailored prevention plan are unnecessary"}}
questions.rationale: Bed-exit alarms are monitoring/alert tools, not physical barriers. Fall prevention should be individualized and layered; an alarm does not replace risk assessment, assistance, toileting plans, environmental measures, or other indicated interventions.
questions.source_detail: AHRQ PSNet describes bed alarms as devices used to notify staff when a patient attempts to get out of bed; they are an alerting intervention rather than a device that physically confines the patient.

questions.stem: Why may a hospital screen visitors for respiratory symptoms during periods of increased community respiratory illness?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"To identify only bacterial infections because viral respiratory illnesses are not relevant to visitor screening","B":"To replace hand hygiene, source control, ventilation, and other infection-prevention measures in the facility","C":"To reduce introduction and spread of respiratory pathogens as one part of layered infection prevention","D":"To permanently exclude all visitors because symptom screening cannot be adjusted to community transmission"}}
questions.rationale: CDC advises healthcare facilities to use layered respiratory infection-prevention practices. Visitors with respiratory symptoms should be advised about source control and may be encouraged to defer non-urgent visits until recovered.
questions.source_name: CDC — Preventing Transmission of Viral Respiratory Pathogens in Healthcare Settings
questions.source_detail: Visitor and respiratory hygiene recommendations; current healthcare guidance accessed 2026-08-14.

questions.stem: Why should a health system avoid setting a nurse manager's span of control solely by maximizing the number of direct reports?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Excessive span can contribute to manager overload and reduce support available to staff and care teams","B":"Span of control affects payroll only and has no documented relationship to managers or staff outcomes","C":"The largest possible span always improves supervision because one manager can standardize every decision","D":"Patient acuity, unit complexity, and staff experience should be ignored when deciding managerial workload"}}
questions.rationale: Research on nurse-manager span of control shows that it is multidimensional and that excessively expanded spans can contribute to manager overload or burnout and lower staff or patient satisfaction. Staffing, complexity, acuity, and manager factors matter.
questions.source_name: Journal of Healthcare Management — Impact of Span of Control on Nurse Managers and Hospital Outcomes
questions.source_detail: 2023 concept analysis, PMID 37159015; consequences of expanded span and multidimensional determinants; accessed 2026-08-14.
